segments.text: Half past three, the day Typhoon Hagibis reached Nagano. Sonae tells one family to leave now. The city's emergency order for their street comes eight hours later. This is the agent team that stands watch.

Japan urges every household to prepare a personal evacuation timeline: who does what, at which official alert level. That means reading the hazard map for your address, finding which site is designated for which disaster, and agreeing who acts. The work itself is the barrier.

And the people least able to do that work are the ones who die. In Japan's recent floods, sixty five to eighty percent of the dead were aged sixty five or over. Often a parent, alone in the family home, hours away from their children.

Typhoon Hagibis, twenty nineteen. At fifteen thirty, Nagano's first ever emergency heavy rain warning. The riverside advisory came at eighteen hundred; the emergency order at twenty three forty, in darkness. At eight past one the river came over the bank at Hoyasu, and the district flooded to roof height. All of it was public.

This is Sonae. One address, and a few sentences about your family. A Cartographer reads the statutory hazard maps. A Planner drafts the timeline, tuned to a grandmother's knees. An adversarial Verifier re-derives every claim from official data. You approve it once. From here, Sonae is authorized to act.
Now the replay, driven event by event from the official record. The day before landfall: level one. Charge the phone. Pack the medication. While the sky is clear.

Saturday afternoon, the river reaches advisory levels. Level two. And here the verifier earns its keep: the draft told the son to skip level three, then escalate to level three. A contradiction, in an instruction read while frightened. Rejected, corrected to level four, then sent.

Half past three. The emergency heavy rain warning — formally level five for rainfall. But level five means protect yourself where you are, and the guidance is to finish evacuating while you can. So Sonae pushes the plan's level four step, approved in advance by the family. Complete the evacuation now. The draft cited a Nagano City order for this district; none existed yet. Rejected, corrected, sent. Sunset is seventeen sixteen — there is still light to walk in.

Then, discipline. Bulletins the plan already covers; the Sentinel stands by through all of them. It is not always right alone. In an earlier run kept in the same journal, it read this level four advisory as level five — and a deterministic guard clamped it down. The model does not get the last word.

The eight fifty bulletin reports upstream overtopping that began at twenty past eight. Level five. Confirm everyone is out, and nobody goes back in. The dashboard opens a check-in for each family member.

Twenty three forty: the emergency evacuation order. At eight past one, the river came over the bank at their doorstep. Sonae's verified push went out at fifteen thirty — eight hours and ten minutes earlier. On the plan's own allowance, a family leaving then reaches the shelter by half past five, in daylight.

After the water, Japanese neighborhoods confirm safety with paper name lists. Sonae replaces the paper, not the neighbors. It hands the chairman an ordered route: first Kazuo, who cannot walk; then Isamu, eighty eight, still unconfirmed.

Historical replay, real pipeline, invented family — every excerpt here is committed in the repository. An alert app broadcasts the same words to everyone. Sonae holds a plan the family approved, and binds official signals to it. Unverified prose is never sent. The official signal is relayed verbatim rather than silenced.

Under the hood: a self-correcting Strands graph builds the plan, a verified pipeline runs the watch, typed JSON between agents, flight recorder hooks on every tool call. Deployed on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, state synced to S3, heartbeat through EventBridge and Lambda — verified, then paused. With no new events a cycle exits before a model is created. Zero tokens. Boring is the job.

Every hazard and alert input comes from public government data. Built for Japan, and adaptable wherever official hazard feeds exist. Sonae. Because the next Hagibis is already forming, and every family deserves someone on watch.
